We're really excited about this year Space Apps Challenge.
summary: SATIT Orbital is a game that lets students design, launch and operate a complete space mission, and feel every engineering trade-off along the way. Players choose one of five missions, from a beginner CubeSat to a Mars weather orbiter, then build a spacecraft part by part while live gauges track mass, power, budget, data, communications and delta-v. They pick an orbit and a rocket, choose ground stations, and fly the mission in a real-time 3D view where solar storms, space debris and budget cuts force crew decisions. A debrief explains which requirements were met, why, and which change would have helped, and links each mission to real NASA missions. The game follows NASA's mission-design process: its phases map to the user, space, launch and ground segments; difficulty mirrors Mission Design Lab study levels; rank follows JPL's Concept Maturity Levels. It supports solo play with an AI crew, co-op for up to four players, spectators, a daily challenge, classroom mode for teachers, a guided first mission and a Thai language option. Scores go to a leaderboard automatically and are verified by replaying each mission on the server.
details:
What it does
SATIT Orbital is a playable model of how a space mission comes together. Each mission has a goal and hard requirements, and every requirement is checked against the player's design and against what actually happens in flight. There is rarely one right answer: different combinations of parts, orbits and rockets can reach the same goal, at different costs. Play it free: https://satit-orbital.deweysworld.app

How it works: five phases, four NASA mission segments

  1. Objective (user segment): choose a mission (CubeSat Classroom, Wildfire Watch, Lunar Relay, Asteroid Scout or Red Planet Weather), a game mode and a study level, then read the requirements and the budget.
  2. Hangar (space segment): pick a structure, solar array, battery, radio, computer, pointing system, engine and science instruments. The spacecraft is built in 3D as you go. Every part shows how it changes mass, power, cost, data and delta-v, and crew characters explain each problem in plain language ("the cameras collect 180 Gb a day but the radio sends 20").
  3. Launch & orbit (launch segment): choose an orbit (sun-synchronous, geostationary, near-rectilinear halo, Earth-Moon L2, flyby, Mars orbits and more), each shown in 3D with its coverage, lifetime, signal strength and delta-v cost, and a rocket that can lift your mass there. For low Earth orbit the revisit time is calculated from the orbit's altitude and the width of the camera's swath, so a wide-swath camera (MODIS-like, about 1 day) revisits sooner than a sharp narrow one (Landsat-like, about 15 days). Then watch the launch.
  4. Operate (ground segment): pick ground stations (a university antenna, a commercial network or the Deep Space Network), then fly the mission day by day. Instruments slow down when power runs short, data is lost when storage fills, and emergencies (solar storms, micrometeoroid strikes, ground outages, reaction-wheel failures, debris, budget cuts) need a crew decision. Each one ends with a short "why it matters" lesson.
  5. Debrief: requirements met or missed and why, a score for science delivered, objectives, efficiency and decision quality, specific suggestions ("an X-band radio would have sent 10 times more data"), real NASA missions with similar goals, and the leaderboard. A ranked mission is sent to the leaderboard automatically when it ends.

Playing together, and in class

  • Up to four players share one mission as Commander, Engineer, Scientist and Ops & Comms, on one device or online. Each role owns different parts of the spacecraft, crew members can suggest changes to parts they don't own, and emergencies are decided by vote. Solo players get an AI crew whose votes reflect each role's priorities.
  • Friends can watch an online mission live as spectators (read-only).
  • Teams can compete with a shared challenge code that gives everyone the same emergencies, and there is a Daily Challenge: one shared mission per day with its own leaderboard.
  • Classroom mode for teachers: a random class code (no names, no emails, no accounts), a class table and a printable report.
  • Any saved run can be replayed on the operations screen. Replays of a daily board or a new challenge unlock after it closes, so nobody can copy a leader's run.

Educational value
The game is built for beginners: no prior knowledge is assumed, every warning explains the cause, and three study levels add complexity gradually. A guided first mission walks a new player through every phase, and there is a Thai language option. Players learn by experimenting: they can fly an imperfect design, see exactly what went wrong, redesign and fly again. Earning two or more stars raises the player's Concept Maturity Level, from "Cocktail Napkin" to "Point Design".

How we used NASA data and resources
The phases follow the four mission segments in "Design and Develop Science Missions". Rank follows the JPL Concept Maturity Levels, and the study levels mirror Mission Design Lab (Office Hours, Trade Study, Point Design). The orbits come from the families GMAT models (low Earth, geostationary, lunar, halo, interplanetary). From "A Learning Game About Telescopes" we took the idea that goals drive engineering choices and that the game should show real NASA missions like yours. CubeSat Classroom follows CubeSat 101 and the CubeSat Design Specification Rev. 14.1 (1U up to 2 kg, 3U up to 6 kg). Mission Viz inspired the orbit views. The part numbers are game-balance values, not NASA data, but the relationships between mass, power, data, distance and cost are realistic.

Tools and technology

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no build step; Three.js for the real-time 3D views; Web Audio for synthesized sound effects (no audio files).
  • Cloudflare Workers for hosting, D1 for the leaderboard, classes and one-time seeds, and Durable Objects for online co-op rooms and spectators over WebSockets.
  • A deterministic simulation engine shared by the browser and the server. The server hands out a random seed for each ranked run and replays every mission from its design, seed and decisions to verify the score.
  • Automated unit and API tests on GitHub Actions.
  • Code repository: https://github.com/deweyyyyy/satit-orbital

What makes it creative
The spacecraft you see in 3D is literally the one you designed: wings, dish, engine and instruments change with every choice. The crew talks back, emergencies have real consequences, and the debrief tells you which single change would have made the difference.

Factors we considered
Accessibility (keyboard play, screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support, mute); privacy (the leaderboard stores only generated callsigns, and classes are random codes, never names); offline use (the game plays without the server, but offline runs are not ranked); fairness (server-verified scores and one-time seeds); and honesty about simplification (part numbers are game-balance values).

Added after the demo video
The demo video shows the core game, which is unchanged. After it was recorded we added the automatic verified leaderboard, the Daily Challenge, replays, classroom mode, spectators, the guided first mission, the Thai language option, a result card (PNG) and the calculated revisit times.

Origin of this project
The original repository is https://github.com/deweyyyyy/satit-orbital. The version first submitted to Space Apps on November 14 is preserved as the git tag v1.0-submitted (also the branch "submitted"), and provenance.json lists a fingerprint of every file in it. The game is also reachable at https://satit-orbital.deweytng.workers.dev and https://satit-orbital.deweysworld.app which hosted on Cloudflare Workers.

How our team made it
We chose the Space Mission Design challenge and decided what the game should be: a game that feels like a real mission-control game, not a web page (we rejected the first page-style design and asked for a game-style interface with 3D). We set the direction and priorities throughout: the mission scenarios, the use of NASA's mission segments, Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab levels, hosting on Cloudflare with a leaderboard and online co-op, the last-day features, and keeping the project open source with a clear record of its origin. We asked for fact-checks of the game's numbers against NASA sources and had errors corrected (for example the CubeSat mass limits). We tested the game, produced the demo video with teammate, and submitted it.

Use of SI
We used Claude (Anthropic), an SI tool, for ideation, research, game-balance analysis, coding, UI and visual design, sound design, translation and writing, working under our direction. This includes the Thai translation (machine-assisted, not yet proofread by a native speaker), the guided first mission text, the server features and the orbit revisit model. Each source file says so in its header, the web page carries an "si-assistance" meta tag, the title screen shows a visible "SI-assisted" notice, and the README describes the use in detail. No SI-generated image, video or audio files are included: graphics and sounds are produced at runtime by SI-assisted code. The game itself does not call any SI service; the AI crew follows fixed rules.
